DNA polymerase. The primary enzyme responsible for replicating DNA by synthesizing new strands in the five-prime to three-prime direction. It catalyzes the addition of nucleotides to a growing strand with high fidelity through proofreading activity that removes mismatched bases. Multiple forms exist across organisms, each specialized for different replication contexts. DNA polymerase catalyzes phosphodiester bond formation between nucleotides moving five-prime to three-prime. It requires a primer—a short RNA or DNA segment—to initiate synthesis, and it cannot start chains entirely anew. The substrate is deoxyribonucleotide triphosphates, with energy coming from the release of pyrophosphate. Built-in three-prime to five-prime exonuclease activity checks and removes mismatches, yielding approximately one error per ten billion bases. Processivity, the number of nucleotides the polymerase can add before dissociating, varies by polymerase type from one to more than one thousand nucleotides. In E. coli there are three polymerases—Pol I, II, and III—with Pol III being the main replication enzyme and Pol I filling gaps left by primer removal. In eukaryotes, Pol alpha-primase starts replication, Pol delta synthesizes the lagging strand, and Pol epsilon synthesizes the leading strand. DNA replication demands extraordinary accuracy to preserve genetic fidelity across cell divisions. DNA polymerase emerged as evolution's solution—a machine that both reads the template strand and verifies its own work in real time. The enzyme's inability to initiate chains without a primer, which might seem like a limitation, is actually a feature that allows cells to recognize replication boundaries and control the process.
